questions.explanation: Adding durations converts both to their common type, the coarsest unit that represents both exactly, which here is `minutes`. So `2h` becomes 120 minutes and the sum is `minutes{150}`. Adding the raw counts, 2 and 30, would ignore the units, which the type system prevents.

A duration converts implicitly only when no precision can be lost: to a finer integer unit, or to any floating-point rep. Converting `1500ms` to integer `seconds` would drop 500 ms, so it needs `duration_cast`, which is why (3) is ill-formed and (4) is fine.

`duration_cast` converts the representation by truncating toward zero, so -1500 ms becomes -1 s. `floor` rounds toward negative infinity and gives -2 s. For positive values the two agree, which is why the difference is easy to miss.

It throws, because February 31 does not exist
questions.explanation: Adding months to a `year_month_day` changes the month and keeps the day number. The result is February 31, 2024, which is a representable but invalid date, so `ok()` is false and `day()` is still 31. Nothing clamps and nothing throws; you must call `ok()` and decide what to do.

Dividing one duration by another converts both to their common type and divides the counts in the common rep. For `1500ms / 1s` the rep is integral, so the quotient is 1500 / 1000, which is 1. When one operand has a `double` rep, the common rep is `double` and the quotient is 1.5.

questions.prompt: Is this program well-formed in C++23?
options: No: the addition overflows the signed representation, which is not a constant expression
Yes, but `t` has an unspecified value
questions.explanation: The representation of `nanoseconds` is a signed integer, and duration addition is ordinary integer addition on it, so exceeding the maximum is signed overflow, which is undefined behavior. A `constexpr` initializer must be a constant expression, and undefined behavior is not one, so the program is ill-formed and the compiler rejects it. At run time the same overflow would silently be undefined behavior; there is no saturation or wraparound guarantee.

questions.prompt: What does this program print in C++20 or later?
options: `00`: an invalid date has no `sys_days` value
questions.explanation: February 30 is not a valid date, so `ok()` is false. The conversion to `sys_days` is nonetheless specified when the year and month are valid: it gives the first of the month plus the day number minus one. For February 2023 that is March 2, so the comparison is true and the output is `01`. Only an invalid year or month leaves the result unspecified.

questions.prompt: In the `America/New_York` zone, clocks went from 02:00 to 03:00 on 2024-03-10. What does the standard specify for this program, assuming a time zone database is available?
options: It prints `gap`: constructing a `zoned_time` from a nonexistent local time throws
It prints `2024-03-10 03:30:00 EDT`: the time is moved forward by the length of the gap
It prints `2024-03-10 01:30:00 EST`: the earlier offset is used
Undefined behavior: the local time does not exist
questions.explanation: A local time inside a daylight saving gap maps to no instant. When the `zoned_time` constructor has to pick an instant from such a `local_time` and no `choose` argument was given, it throws `nonexistent_local_time`; the two silent options in the other answers are not behaviors the library provides. The ambiguous case, an hour that occurs twice when clocks go back, throws `ambiguous_local_time` unless `choose::earliest` or `choose::latest` is passed.
